title: The King of the Ants
sourceAuthor: Richard Wilhelm, editor; Frederick H. Martens, translator
note: A new adaptation of “The King of the Ants.” The source identifies it as a tale from the Tang Dai Tsung Schu; this version omits the source’s destructive ending.

rights.basis: Source edition published in 1921 and identified as public domain by Project Gutenberg.

artLabel: Tiny riders and banners parade around an ink saucer on a scholar’s desk.
scenes: A traveling scholar rented a quiet house in Emmet Village. One evening, hundreds of knights no taller than rice grains galloped across his room.
Tiny servants raised tents and tables beside his ink saucer, which they called the Purple Lake. Musicians played; dancers turned; nets caught little red fish.
At last their king arrived in scarlet and purple. Proud of his grand court, he laughed at the poor scholar and offered him a lowly place among the servants.
The scholar shut his book with a clap. Riders, cooks, banners, and king scattered through a crack in the wall.
Outside, he found an enormous green ants’ nest. He left it undisturbed and returned to his studies.
After seeing a kingdom fit inside one room, his own troubles no longer seemed quite so large.

pageArt.alt: A tiny ant king arrives with miniature riders and banners around the scholar’s ink saucer.
The scholar kneels beside a great green ants’ nest and chooses to leave it undisturbed.
